Nor is the incidence of the consumer-law microsystem exhausted in the isolated text of the CDC itself. Its normative structure is open to coordination with other protective sources, because it is not a closed and self-sufficient code, but a system functionally oriented toward the maximum protection of the consumer. This openness is particularly important in complex contexts, such as those of platforms and immaterial objects of consumption, in which adequate protection depends on an articulated reading of constitutional, civil, informational, contractual and regulatory norms. Marques addresses this point by stating that the CDC must be understood as "a subjectively specific codification, a partial codification, a functional and open codification", adding that, by virtue of its art. 7, it "lets itself be permeated by any other law protective of the consumer" <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 681)</2>. The function of this openness, however, is not to relativize consumer-law protection, but to reinforce it. That is why the author observes that, in the CDC system, art. 7 acts as an "updating interface", integrating into the microsystem the rights ensured by external legislation, "but not the limits to those rights" <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1120-1121)</4>. Coordination among sources is thus carried out in favor of the protected vulnerability, and not as a privatist escape route. <5>↩</5>

Section 6.1.2.1 · pp. 520 to 534
<1>6.1.2.1 On the physical frontiers of sovereignty: Vanguard as a case study </1>

The case of the <1>anti-cheat</1> <2>Vanguard</2> exposes, in a particularly clear way, a qualitative mutation in the private governance of the immaterial object of consumption. It is no longer merely a matter of <3>p. 521</3> conditioning enjoyment of the game on internal rules of conduct, progression or permanence in the ecosystem, but of projecting the demands of competitive integrity onto the consumer's own material infrastructure.

When the protection of the IOC's competitive environment comes to depend on software loaded at <1>kernel</1> level, that is, in the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system, the platform ceases merely to occupy the computer as the contingent support of a ludic experience and begins to reorganize, in its own favor, the practical regime of availability, risk, surveillance and control of the equipment. <2>Riot</2>'s own official communications show that <3>Vanguard</3> is presented as a system composed of a <4>client</4> and a <5>driver</5> in <6>kernel</6> mode, started at the computer's boot and maintained as a structural condition of enjoyment in more than one game ecosystem, with the possibility of preventing use of the service if it is disabled or removed<7><8>528</8></7>.

This fact shifts the legal problem beyond intuitive irritation with “intrusive” software. What is at stake is the redefinition of the material frontiers of the user's sovereignty over their own equipment. <1>Riot</1> contractually admits the possibility of actively monitoring the use of its services not only on its own servers, but also on the consumer's computer or device<2><3>529</3></2>, and provides that the anti-cheat software may <4>p. 522</4> remain running in the background on the device<5><6>530</6></5>. As a result, the protection of the IOC does not remain confined to the concrete moment of the match. It becomes a vector of preventive and continued governance over the technical environment in which the game will be run, reaching the machine even before the specific decision to enjoy. In a later update, the company itself makes explicit that its concern is no longer limited to the loaded operating system, but reaches the prior stage of <7>hardware</7> initialization, justifying the hardening of integrity requirements on the basis of risks detected in early phases of <8>boot</8><9><10>531</10></9>. The private sovereignty of the platform, in other words, ceases to govern only the game and begins to contest the minimum conditions of reliability of the user's own machine.

Under the vocabulary of security, this expansion usually appears as if it were simple technical inevitability. But the discourse of security does not, by itself, neutralize the legal relevance of the architecture adopted. In the digital environment, storage, sharing and <1>p. 523</1> persistent monitoring of information represent a threat to privacy serious enough to require specific normative containment, above all in a surveillance society in which data processing becomes a central asset of business models and of behavioral control <2>Mendes</2><3>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69; p. 73; p. 82)</3><4><5>532</5></4>. The security argument itself may function as a legitimizer of the expansion of private powers over fundamental spheres of informational life, especially when the demand for data and structural surveillance are normalized by routine and barely intelligible acceptances <6>Mendes</6><7>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70-71)</7><8><9>533</9></8>. It is not enough, therefore, to invoke the fight against cheating as a magic word. The problem becomes one of proportionality, necessity, transparency and justifiability of the degree of technical interference demanded of the consumer.

This perception is reinforced when one observes that invasive architectures are neither neutral nor merely instrumental. Monitoring technologies and algorithmic governance incorporate human choices and restructure power relations over the user, allowing veiled control and the favoring of their own interests by those who dominate the digital infrastructure <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 24; p. 30-31)</2><3><4>534</4></3>. In the network, the accumulation of traces and the expansion of surveillance <5>p. 524</5> make the individual's vulnerability deeper, because less perceptible control mechanisms come to bear on their private sphere and on their practical freedom, requiring that they preserve some command over the accuracy, the handlers and the uses of the information that describes them <6>Costa</6><7>(Costa, 2018, p. 26; p. 41; p. 43)</7><8><9>535</9></8>. <10>Vanguard</10> is paradigmatic precisely because this reorganization of power does not appear as a side effect of the service, but as a central condition of its legitimate functioning according to the platform itself.

That is why the question is not resolved by privacy understood in a shallow sense, as if the problem were only a one-off intrusion into the intimate space. The protection of personal data and of informational autonomy serves precisely to protect the person against mechanisms of control, classification and conditioning that bear on their freedom and their self-determination. Intensive data processing and the construction of electronic representations of the individual do not merely record conduct; they come to organize predictions, profiles and conditionings that compress the practical sphere of freedom and make informational power legally relevant <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 26; p. 149; p. 164)</2><3><4>536</4></3>. When organized data <5>p. 525</5> function as operational substitutes for the person, surveillance ceases to be a simple administrative instrument and becomes a potential mechanism for affecting individuality, autonomy and the free development of personality <6>Doneda</6><7>(Doneda, 2020, p. 25-26; p. 40; p. 93)</7><8><9>537</9></8>. Demanding persistent, deep and opaque access to the user's computing environment, therefore, is not a mere technical detail of the service; it is a controllable form of bearing on the person.

In a constitutional key, this suffices to rule out any attempt to treat the technical intensification of private power as an enclave immune to the order of fundamental rights. Even though the agent remains private, the intensification of control over hardware, informational flows and practical conditions of use remains subject to the protective filter that radiates from the Constitution over the entire legal order <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 205; p. 531)</2><3><4>538</4></3>. The constitutional order remains in the room precisely because the platform does not act only upon <5>p. 526</5> an abstract thing, but upon the consumer's practical sphere, their equipment, their privacy and their real possibility of enjoying the object or not without submitting the rest of the machine to mutable private standards of integrity.

As a brief restatement of the foundation already laid in the previous item, the theory of the effect of fundamental rights remains useful as a reminder that the technical intensification of private power over the user's sphere does not make it legally invisible merely because it is exercised outside the State. If fundamental rights radiate effects over the entire legal order, including through their objective effect and the requirement that private law be interpreted in conformity with the Constitution, then private structures of monitoring, control and technical interference also remain subject to this protective filter <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 205; p. 531)</2>. The value of the reference, here, is merely functional. It serves to reaffirm that the intensified exercise of private power over hardware, informational flows and practical conditions of use does not automatically convert the agent into the State, but neither does it place it in an enclave immune to the protective incidence of fundamental rights. Sarlet's lesson recalls that, when the supplier's technical power deeply reaches the consumer's practical sphere, the constitutional order remains in the room. <3>↩</3>

“10.2. Will the Riot Services remain the same? (No. Like Kha’zix, they will evolve.) In an effort to constantly improve the Riot Services, promote the evolution of our games and keep the Riot Services safe, fun and secure, you agree that we may change, modify, update, suspend, “nerf” or restrict your access to any features or parts of the Riot Services, including Virtual Products (for example, we may change some features of Virtual Products for regulatory or legal reasons or to improve the game experience), and we may require you to download and install <1>software</1> and updates to any <2>software</2> needed to support the Riot Services, at any time, without liability to you, to the extent permitted by law. You also understand and agree that these changes or updates to the Riot Services may change the system specifications needed to play our games and, in that case, you, and not Riot Games, will be responsible for purchasing any additional software or hardware needed to access and play our games. You also understand and agree that we may use background patches to automatically update our games and software with or without prior notice.” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Riot's Terms of Service provide the general contractual framework through which the supplier seeks to legitimize, on the one hand, practices of monitoring and running anti-cheat <1>software</1> on the user's computer or device and, on the other, broad powers of technical modification of the service. The document expressly provides that <2>Riot</2> may actively monitor the use of its services both on its own servers and on the consumer's computer or device, including for the prevention of cheating and <3>hacking</3>, as well as require the installation of anti-cheat <4>software</4> capable of operating in the background. Along the same expansive logic, the Terms establish that the company may change, update, suspend, restrict features, require the download and installation of <5>software</5> and updates needed for the functioning of the service, and also transfer to the user the burden of acquiring additional <6>software</6> or <7>hardware</7> if the technical specifications change. In parallel, the contractual wording seeks to reduce the supplier's financial exposure by stating that the services are offered as is, without broad warranties, assigning to the user responsibility for use and limiting Riot's liability for losses and damages, including in relation to failures linked to not installing updates or to maintaining minimum system requirements. The relevance of the document lies, therefore, in showing that the platform's very contractual structure seeks to frame in advance the submission of the consumer's equipment to additional layers of surveillance, compulsory technical adaptation and shifting of risk, which speaks directly to the problem of the CDC's control over contractual shielding clauses and excessive transfer of burdens to the user <8>Riot Games</8><9>(Riot Games, 2024e)</9>. <10>↩</10>

These are the acronyms for <1>Basic Input/Output System</1> and <2>Unified Extensible Firmware Interface.</2> They designate the basic software interfaces that reside in the hardware and are responsible for preparing the machine for the start of the operating system. They constitute the deepest layers of control of the computer, onto which the platform may project demands of technical conformity. <3>↩</3>

At the contractual level, this intensification appears in an especially raw form. Riot's Terms of Service not only admit active monitoring on the user's device and the running of anti-cheat software in the background, but also reserve to the company the power to change, update, restrict features, require software and compulsory updates, redistribute to the user the costs of technical adaptation and limit its own financial exposure<1><2>539</2></1>. The general contractual framework thus seeks to frame in advance the submission of the consumer's equipment to additional layers of surveillance, compulsory adaptation and shifting of risk<3><4>540</4></3>. This is the point at which the case ceases to be merely a discussion about fighting fraud and becomes a classic problem of the supplier's contractual shielding in the face of an invasive technical architecture that it itself imposes.

At the empirical level, too, the overflow of the IOC onto the consumer's hardware is too hard to hide. <1>Riot</1> itself, in documents addressed to developers and to users of <2>VALORANT</2>, admits that <3>Vanguard</3> may block third-party applications, require <4>p. 527</4> sensitive changes in <5>BIOS</5> or <6>UEFI</6><7><8>541</8></7>, impose the enabling of <9>TPM 2.0</9>, <10>Secure Boot</10>, <11>IOMMU</11>, memory integrity and other security layers, besides recognizing that incorrect changes to these settings may cause serious problems on the computer<12><13>542</13></12>. This is no small thing. The platform conditions the enjoyment of the immaterial object on the prior conformity of the machine's technical ecosystem with private standards of integrity and compatibility unilaterally defined by it. The user's computer comes, functionally, to be administered as an extension of the game's competitive environment.

The public reaction to <1>Vanguard</1> confirms that the problem was socially perceived precisely in these terms. In specialized press coverage, the controversy revolved around the <2>always-on</2> character of the <3>anti-cheat</3>, its loading at <4>kernel</4> level from system startup, the fear of persistent surveillance and the interference with<5><6>543</6></5> <7>p. 528</7> non-game uses of the equipment<8><9>544</9></8>. The value of this material lies not in proving, alone, any forensic thesis, but in showing that the criticism did not arise as marginal paranoia. The case was publicly understood as a genuine dispute over the legitimate limits of the private governance exercised by the platform over the consumer's machine. Public perception does not start from nothing; it starts from the observation of how hard the company strives to enter the subject's technical home under a generic discourse of security, arrogating to itself powers of inspection and direct effect whose potential for intrusion is substantially greater than the initial scope of its responsibility for the object supplied.

Critical and specialized secondary sources help organize why a <2>kernel</2>-level <1>anti-cheat</1> is qualitatively different from ordinary <3>software</3>. They converge in pointing to three axes of concern: systemic security, through enlargement of the attack surface; structural instability, because errors in such privileged components may reach the entire operating system; and persistent surveillance, since the software may remain active from the <4>p. 529</4> machine's startup<5><6>545</6></5>. The most important point here is comparative: the <7>kernel-</7><8>level always-on</8> architecture does not appear as an inevitable fact of every <9>anti-cheat</9>, but as a technical choice that intensifies the degree of intrusion, dependence and risk assumed by the consumer in the name of the ecosystem's competitive integrity.

This perception also materializes in reports of instability and technical conflict. On <1>Microsoft Q&A</1>, there are recurring records of blue screens, severe freezes and failures associated with the file <2>vgk.sys</2> or with the technical ecosystem in which <3>Vanguard</3> operates, including at moments when the game was not even open<4><5>546</5></4>. The reports document, in a <6>p. 530</6> technically situated environment, the recurrence of risks radiating to the system as a whole, and not only to the ludic experience. The argument does not depend on absolute demonstration of universal harm; it is enough to show that the required architecture transfers to the consumer a legally relevant systemic risk.

Even more concretely, community reports illustrate the conflict between <1>Vanguard</1> and legitimate, ordinary and non-ludic uses of the computer. There are incompatibilities with <3>hardware</3> monitoring and management <2>software</2>, interference with study routines and conflict with legitimate system debugging tools<4><5>547</5></4>. Although they have merely illustrative value, these sources are empirically useful because they materialize something central to the dogmatics of the case: the computer ceases to function as a neutral support of the game and comes to be reorganized according to private criteria of tolerance and priority defined by the platform. In a <6>p. 531</6> consumer-law key, this is devastating for any attempt to treat the problem as a mere internal technical whim of the supplier.

There are also sources that systematize the case already through the lens of consumer rights and public perception of risk, associating <1>Vanguard</1> with persistent technical presence, absence of a real alternative of refusal, expansion of control over the machine and continuous functioning outside the strict moment of play<2><3>548</3></2>. The point is important because it shows that the dispute is neither merely technical nor merely cultural. It is already perceived as a consumer-rights problem, precisely because the enjoyment of the IOC comes to be conditioned on a material subordination of the user's equipment to private criteria of security and compatibility.

Even the most extreme reports of possible <1>bricking</1><2><3>549</3></2> or severe loss of availability of the equipment have illustrative usefulness for the argument, even though they do not authorize conclusive forensic statements<4><5>550</5></4>. Their value lies in showing how the risk radiating <6>p. 532</6> to the hardware forms part of the empirical reception of the case and speaks directly to the thesis that the governance of the IOC may go beyond the game environment and reach the material functionality of the machine itself. It is the limit-form of the problem. Not the only one, nor necessarily the most frequent, but the one that makes it impossible to pretend we are only talking about “just another game software”.

Nor would it be honest to fail to recognize that there exists, even among the harshest criticisms, a consistent technical-cultural discourse in defense of more invasive measures, according to which fighting cheats in competitive games involves an asymmetric dispute and continuous escalation, which would make understandable the adoption of deep countermeasures by the platform<1><2>551</2></1>. This counterpoint is useful because it prevents an easy caricature of the practice. The serious legal question was never whether there is a legitimate interest in preserving competitive integrity; of course there is. The question is another: whether this interest suffices to authorize, without reinforced control, the expansion of the supplier's technical power over the material base of the consumer's equipment.

Then the normative parameters of containment come in. The CDC does not allow <1>Vanguard</1> to be made invisible as if it were a mere engineering option. Products and services placed on the market may not entail risks to health or safety beyond those normal and foreseeable from <2>p. 533</2> their nature and enjoyment<3><4>552</4></3>, and the supplier may not place on the market a product or service that it knows or should know to present a high degree of harmfulness or dangerousness<5><6>553</6></5>. In limit cases, liability itself for design defects or for insufficient or inadequate information about use and risks<7><8>554</8></7> reopens the door to treating invasive software as a defective or inadequately informed product. The point here is not to automatically assert the total unlawfulness of the <10>kernel</10> <9>anti-cheat</9>, but to refuse its legal immunization. If the architecture intensifies systemic risk, enlarges the attack surface, requires deep technical conformations and may radiate instability to the equipment, then it enters the radar of consumer-law safety control.

The LGPD reinforces this picture without requiring any regulatory symposium. The data processing linked to Vanguard cannot be justified en bloc under the generic heading of “security”, because it must observe a legitimate, specific, explicit and informed purpose<1><2>555</2></1>, necessity, with limitation to the indispensable minimum<3><4>556</4></3>, and transparency, with clear, precise and accessible information<5><6>557</6></5>. It also requires an adequate legal basis<7><8>558</8></7>, is not automatically satisfied by ritualized and generic acceptances<9><10>559</10></9>, and presupposes technical and administrative measures apt for the effective protection of data<11><12>560</12></11>. In other words, the platform cannot invoke security as a totalizing justification while maintaining opacity about the scope, necessity and agents of the processing. Alleged security does not replace legally demonstrated security.

<1>p. 534</1> <2>Vanguard</2> demonstrates that the <3>Lex Plataformae</3> may functionally overflow the immaterial space of the game and radiate concrete effects onto the consumer's material sovereignty over their own equipment. The private protection of competitive integrity comes to reorganize the availability, compatibility, startup, surveillance and risk of the hardware, shifting technical costs and burdens to the user and compressing their margin of practical self-determination. It is not a matter of denying the legitimacy of fighting fraud, but of denying that this legitimacy authorizes, by itself, deep, preventive, persistent and opaque technical governance over another's machine. Where the platform requires the consumer's computer to become functionally subordinate to its private layers of integrity, the law is not facing a technical detail. It is facing an exemplary case of private expansion of power that requires containment through safety, proportionality, transparency, liability and control.

In the official support communications dedicated to <1>League of Legends</1> and to <2>VALORANT</2>, <3>Riot</3> itself describes <4>Vanguard</4> as security <5>software</5> composed of a client active while the game is running and a driver in <6>kernel</6> mode, that is, installed in the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system, with access far greater than that of ordinary applications <7>Riot Games</7><8>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</8>. In both explanations, the company also clarifies that <9>Vanguard</9> is started at the computer's boot, so that its presence and functioning are not restricted to the exact moment of the match, but form part in advance of the material environment in which the enjoyment of the IOC will take place <10>Riot Games</10><11>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</11>. In the case of <12>League of Legends</12>, <13>Riot</13> makes explicit that <14>Vanguard</14> must remain active not only during the match, but also whenever the client is open, and that its deactivation, uninstallation or unauthorized interaction prevents use of the game; in the case of <15>VALORANT</15>, it further states that deactivating the system requires restarting the machine to restore the possibility of playing <16>Riot Games</16><17>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</17>. Both pages also recognize practical consequences that go beyond the game executable in the strict sense, by admitting the blocking of elements considered vulnerable on the user's computer, the conditioning of enjoyment on the machine's adaptation to security standards defined by the platform and the possibility of impact on the very functioning of the device when there are unexpected interactions among client, driver and system <18>Riot Games</18><19>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</19>. Taken together, the sources are empirically valuable because they show, in the institutional voice of the supplier itself and in more than one game ecosystem, that the competitive protection of the IOC is implemented through deep technical access, early loading and structural permanence in the consumer's computing environment, which reinforces the thesis that the platform unilaterally redefines the material conditions of enjoyment of the immaterial good already acquired, reorganizing availability, compatibility, startup and ordinary use of the equipment itself <20>Riot Games</20><21>(Riot Games, 2024r; Riot Games, 2024t)</21>. <22>↩</22>

“9.1. Does Riot monitor me while I use the Riot Services? (Yes. Read the Privacy Policy to learn more.) We may actively monitor the use of the Riot Services (but we have no obligation to do so), both on our own servers and on your computer or device, for a variety of different reasons, including preventing cheating and hacking, reducing toxic player behavior, and improving the Riot Services. Please make sure to read the Privacy Policy for important details about how we obtain and process information relating to the use of the Riot Services.” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>. <3>↩</3>

“9.2. Does Riot run programs on my device while I am not using the Riot Services? (We may, for limited anti-cheat purposes.) To prevent cheating and hackers, we may require you to install anti-cheat <1>software</1> to play our games. This <2>software</2> may run in the background on your device.” <3>Riot Games</3><4>(Riot Games, 2024e)</4>. <5>↩</5>

In an institutional statement prepared by its security and privacy teams, <1>Riot</1> builds an explicit defense of the invasive architecture of <2>Vanguard</2> in the face of public criticism about privacy and security. The text seeks to justify <3>kernel</3>-level access on the argument that more sophisticated cheats no longer operate only in the ordinary space of <4>software</4>, but advance onto deeper layers of the operating system; therefore, according to the company, an <5>anti-cheat</5> restricted to user mode would be technically insufficient to preserve so-called competitive integrity. Along the same line, Riot states that Vanguard is composed of client, driver and platform, that the kernel-mode driver is recognized as a condition of the machine's trustworthiness and that it is started at system boot precisely to prevent the prior loading of cheating mechanisms. At the same time, the communication tries to reduce the perception of risk by maintaining that the driver does not, by itself, collect or transmit information from the user's computer and by highlighting internal and external security reviews, as well as a bounty program for identifying vulnerabilities. The relevance of the document lies in showing, with clarity, the rhetorical and justificatory movement by which the supplier itself presents the expansion of its technical power over the consumer's machine as a necessary consequence of protecting the game's competitive environment. In other words, invasiveness is not denied; it is assumed, framed and legitimized by the company as an acceptable cost of the private governance of the IOC, which is central to the legal analysis of the proportionality, controllability and distribution of risks of this architecture <6>Riot Games</6><7>(Riot Games, 2020e)</7>. In an official update published at the end of 2025, <8>Riot</8> makes explicit with even greater adherence the logic of preventive governance that sustains <9>Vanguard</9>. The text states that the company identified a critical flaw in several modern motherboards, capable of allowing the invisible injection of code already in the early stages of the machine's startup, even before the operating system is fully loaded. On the basis of this finding, Riot justifies the hardening of its integrity requirements by maintaining that components loaded earlier in the boot process operate with a higher degree of privilege and, precisely for that reason, may compromise the entire environment before the operating system or the anti-cheat itself can react. Invasive technical architectures of monitoring do not become legally neutral merely because they present themselves as instruments of security, fraud prevention or service integrity. In the digital environment, the constant storage and sharing of information represent a grave threat to fundamental rights, especially privacy, requiring more specific regulatory action to impose limits on abuses of this nature <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69)</2>. The same key is reinforced when contemporary society is described as a genuine surveillance society, permanently directed at data collection, which explains the need to regulate digital relations with a focus on the protection of personal data, privacy and other fundamental rights affected by this technological medium <3>Mendes</3><4>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 73)</4>. In addition, the processing of personal data has become the main asset of a hyperconnected society, serving as raw material for improving businesses and extracting behavioral patterns aimed at classifying and categorizing people, which is why the Law seeks to keep pace with this development through new legislation and new rights aimed at safeguarding fundamental rights <5>Mendes</5><6>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82)</6>. Thus, private forms of intensive monitoring, such as those represented by invasive technologies of continuous surveillance, must be read as an exercise of structurally relevant informational power, apt to attract reinforced legal containment. <7>↩</7>

The discourse of security is not enough, by itself, to legally neutralize invasive monitoring techniques, because it may itself function as a legitimizing vector for the expansion of private powers over fundamental spheres of informational life. In the context following the September 11 attack, a gradual movement of mitigation of privacy and of other fundamental guarantees was consolidated in the name of a growing need for transparency, opening space for companies to begin collecting, selecting and classifying personal data for the purpose of controlling individuals <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>. The same logic appears when the use of platforms and websites is frequently conditioned on the entry of personal data, often without effectively qualified consent of the data subject, such data being subsequently exploited commercially and monetized through advertising and other business models <3>Mendes</3><4>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</4>. In reinforcement, automated processing not only knows human behavior, but shapes it at scale, so that the goal ceases to be merely automating the flow of information about people and comes to include the automation of people themselves <5>Mendes</5><6>(Zuboff apud Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 71)</6>. Private forms of intensive surveillance, therefore, cannot be treated as a neutral technical requirement of system integrity, because their structure and effects reach privacy, self-determination and freedom to a degree sufficient to justify reinforced legal containment. <7>↩</7>

The technical architecture of persistent monitoring is not reducible to an instrumental requirement of efficiency or security, because it incorporates design choices that reorganize power relations over the user. Algorithms and artificial intelligence technologies cannot be understood as ethically neutral instruments, because they are designed by human beings and form part of a broader process of social and moral restructuring of modernity <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 30-31)</2>. The same key deepens when behavioral control comes to be produced through pattern identification, allowing economic and political agents to use algorithmic governance to favor their own interests through the exercise of veiled power over people <3>Costa</3><4>(Costa, 2018, p. 24)</4>. In addition, the Information Society, structured by the accumulation and circulation of data, establishes new situations of power, which is why the individual cannot be treated as a mere data provider, and must retain at least some control over the accuracy of the information, over the subjects who handle it and over its forms of use <5>Costa</5><6>(Costa, 2018, p. 43)</6>. It is precisely this key that matters to the Vanguard case: private forms of intensive monitoring are not a neutral by-product of security <7>software</7>, but an expression of the technical reorganization of power over the user, legally relevant from the standpoint of privacy, autonomy and the containment of invasive architectures. <8>↩</8>

Persistent and invasive monitoring in a private environment constitutes a legally relevant problem not because of some abstract allergy to technique, but because it bears directly on the private sphere and deepens structural asymmetries of power between the user and the agents who control the digital infrastructure. In networked daily life, electronic traces accumulate that are apt to identify the person, influence their relationships, reconstruct their paths and reveal intimate choices and desires, so that surveillance becomes perpetual while the individual remains inserted in this environment, increasing their vulnerability before companies and the State itself <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 26)</2>. The same perception is reinforced when the expansion of surveillance comes accompanied by control mechanisms that are ever less perceptible and more harmful to freedom, which shifts the protection of personal data to the center of the legal problem <3>Costa</3><4>(Costa, 2018, p. 41)</4>. In addition, the private sphere comes to encompass a much broader set of actions, behaviors, opinions, preferences and information over which the individual intends to maintain exclusive control, it being precisely for privacy to protect these life choices against abuses by platforms <5>Costa</5><6>(Costa, 2018, p. 43)</6>. It is precisely this key that matters to the case: persistent and invasive monitoring in a private environment reaches the user's freedom, control over oneself, private sphere and vulnerability to a degree sufficient to require legal containment. <7>↩</7>

Intensive data collection, processing and monitoring do not concern only privacy in the classical sense, as if the legal problem were restricted to the exposure of an isolated intimate space. The broader point lies in protecting the person against forms of control, classification and conditioning that bear on their personal freedom and on their capacity for self-determination. It is in this sense that the protection of personal data is not limited to safeguarding intimacy, but reaches the containment of mechanisms of control and discrimination capable of affecting fundamental dimensions of the individual's freedom <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 26)</2>. Consequently, persistent, deep and opaque forms of monitoring, even when presented as a technical requirement of security or service integrity, cannot be treated as neutral externalities of the platform's functioning. The problem worsens when informational processing ceases merely to record conduct and comes to organize predictions, profiles and conditionings about the person. When the electronic representation of the individual becomes the main visible point of contact for third parties, techniques for predicting behavioral patterns tend to reduce their practical sphere of freedom, because future decisions come to be made on the basis of presumed behaviors and not only of conduct actually carried out <3>Doneda</3><4>(Doneda, 2020, p. 149)</4>. The protection of personal data, in this key, broadens the traditional focus of privacy to reach the various forms of control made possible by the intensive processing of personal information, which requires attention not only to the ostensive trait of the violation, but to the very structure of informational power that emerges from these practices <5>Doneda</5><6>(Doneda, 2020, p. 164)</6>. It is precisely for this reason that invasive monitoring architectures are not exhausted in a technical discussion about <7>software</7>: they also constitute a problem of protecting the person against excessive incursions on their informational autonomy. <8>↩</8>

Contemporary informational surveillance does not act only through external observation of the individual, but through the construction of digital representations apt to influence decisions about credit, health, work, movement and access to opportunities. When organized personal data come to function as a genuine operational substitute for the person, the intensive processing of information ceases to be a mere administrative instrument and becomes a potential mechanism for affecting autonomy, individuality and freedom <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 25-26)</2>. From this perspective, demanding persistent, deep and opaque access to the user's environment does not mean merely gathering data to make a service viable, but establishing an expanded possibility of evaluating, classifying and conditioning their sphere of self-determination. The historical mutation of forms of surveillance itself reinforces this point. Instead of remaining tied only to the physical or psychological observation of the person, surveillance has shifted largely to the plane of personal data, so that a relevant portion of these practices has come to constitute an abusive exercise of power <3>Doneda</3><4>(Doneda, 2020, p. 40)</4>. Hence the centrality of protecting a private sphere in which the person can freely develop their personality, without submission to mechanisms of social control capable of annulling individuality, restricting private autonomy and hindering free personal development <5>Doneda</5><6>(Doneda, 2020, p. 93)</6>. Consequently, persistent monitoring and excessive data processing are not legally indifferent side effects of the digital service, but controllable forms of bearing on the person, which is why their legitimacy depends on reinforced legal containment. <7>↩</7>

<1>6.1.2 </1>On the horizontal effect of fundamental rights and the public relevance of the powers of the Lex Plataformae

The horizontal effect of fundamental rights ceases to seem an abstract theoretical question when one observes that, in contemporary private relations, relevant subjection no longer comes only from the State. It also emerges from private centers of power capable of organizing access, permanence, visibility, reputation, evidence and contestation on a scale sufficient to affect, structurally, the practical freedom and material equality of the subject submitted to the relation. In such contexts, private autonomy cannot function as a screen to shield materially asymmetric arrangements, because the Constitution is not limited to restraining public power, also radiating effects over bonds between private parties when the concentration of power becomes legally relevant <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 51; p. 258; p. 285)</2><3><4>502</4></3>. The private relation remains private, but the fantasy disappears that this <5>p. 513</5> formal qualification, by itself, would make it immune to the normative force of fundamental rights <6>Sarlet</6><7>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 528-529)</7><8><9>503</9></8>.

This reinforced incidence does not require a conceptual statization of the platform, nor confusion between company and public power. The legally relevant point lies in the material density of the power exercised and in the concrete effects it produces on the sphere of the other subject of the relation. When a private agent concentrates economic, technical, informational and organizational power sufficient to condition choices, restrict freedoms and reconfigure the user's practical position, the private nature of the bond is no longer enough to expel the Constitution from the scene <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 61; p. 209; p. 298)</2><3><4>504</4></3>. It is precisely for this reason that the incidence of fundamental rights in relations between private parties becomes more intense in scenarios of structural asymmetry, in which contractual freedom ceases to express a minimally real parity and comes to cover the material dependence of the weaker side <5>Santos</5><6>(Santos, 2019, p. 15; p. 112; p. 132)</6><7><8>505</8></7>.

<1>p. 514</1> It is within this framework that the <2>Lex Plataformae</2> must be understood. It is not reducible to the contract, nor is it confused with an isolated technical instrument, because it designates the coordinated set of rules, procedures and operational standards by which the platform structures the continued enjoyment of the object consumed. Terms of use, internal policies, interface, reputational systems, updating, support and <3>enforcement</3> do not appear there as loose pieces, but as a private regime for the practical ordering of the consumption experience. The platform, thus, does not merely offer utilities; it governs the very conditions of access, permanence, equivalence, intelligibility and contestation of enjoyment, asymmetrically distributing information, evidentiary capacity and powers of unilateral modulation. This suffices to dispel the naive image of the contract as a neutral meeting of equivalent wills and to put the problem back where it really is: in the legal containment of a private power structurally preponderant over the consumer <4>Marques</4><5>(Marques, 2016, p. 42; p. 162)</5><6><7>506</7></6>.

The very clauses of the ecosystem examined make this phenomenon too empirical to be treated as an abstraction. <1>Riot</1> reserves to itself the power to terminate or suspend accounts on the basis of criteria formulated by itself, including in consideration of the “best interest” of its community or its services<2><3>507</3></2>.

<1>p. 515</1> It also provides for bans, suspension, account deletion, hardware bans, content removal, progress resets and functional restrictions<2><3>508</3></2>, extends its discipline to off-platform uses linked to game content<4><5>509</5></4> and radiates penalties from one service to another within the same ecosystem<6><7>510</7></6>.

We are not, therefore, facing a mere technical infrastructure of entertainment, but a private center of governance that disciplines permanence, history, visibility, progression and contestation in an integrated network. The public relevance of this power is not born of grandiloquent metaphor, but of the brute fact that it organizes, on a continued basis, the consumer's practical position in the digital environment.

For this reason, the horizontal effect of fundamental rights does not enter here as an artificial graft, but as a constitutional response to the intensity of the private power concretely exercised. Private autonomy, in a constitutional key, is not an abstract safe-conduct for the material subjection of the user, above all when inequality of power turns formal freedom into an elegant fiction <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 183; p. 286)</2><3><4>511</4></3>. Also for this reason, the <5>p. 516</5> reinforced incidence of fundamental rights in the private sphere does not depend on any rite of transformation of the private party into a “quasi-State”; it is enough to recognize that the threat to freedom, to material equality and to dignity may come from holders of social and economic power intense enough to produce relevant subjection <6>Sarlet</6><7>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 527; p. 529; p. 530)</7><8><9>512</9></8>. In simple terms: the platform remains a private party, but it does not thereby gain a constitutional license to operate as a small jurisdiction immune to control.

This point thickens when one recalls that the Constitution does not tolerate forms of marginalization, blocking and discrimination merely because they are practiced by private agents. The promotion of the good of all without discrimination<1><2>513</2></1>, the protection of honor, image and the personal sphere<3><4>514</4></3>, the inviolability of intimacy, private life, honor and image<5><6>515</6></5>, the inafastability of jurisdiction<7><8>516</8></7> and the prohibition of deprivation of property without due process<9><10>517</10></9> make up, here, a decisive constitutional framework. In platform environments, exclusions, suspensions, removals, reputational erasures and invasive monitoring cannot be treated as technical noise or simple “internal administration of the service”, because they affect the consumer's biographical trajectory, their informational integrity, their practical permanence in the ecosystem and their very capacity to respond to the power that governs them. The problem <11>p. 517</11> is not only patrimonial; it is also one of personality, of practical freedom and of the controllability of private power.

In the digital environment, this reading gains even more density because the exercise of private power also passes through surveillance and the collection, processing and exploitation of personal data. Data are not neutral matter of market circulation, but legally relevant projections of personality, whose protection is linked to human dignity and to informational self-determination <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155-156)</2><3><4>518</4></3>. The information society itself, by intensifying private structures of surveillance and behavioral analysis, required the explicit statement of new fundamental rights and the reinforcement of data protection as a response to the practical erosion of privacy <5>Mendes</5><6>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70; p. 78-79; p. 82- 83)</6><7><8>519</8></7>. When private agents accumulate the capacity to monitor, infer and modulate behaviors in depth, we are no longer facing simple neutral business freedom, but a socially relevant form of power over fundamental goods of the person.

Data protection and the protection of personality rights help demonstrate, on the contemporary Brazilian plane, that the reinforced incidence of fundamental rights on digitally mediated private powers is no longer a remote hypothesis. It is a matter of recognizing that private structures of digital governance bear on privacy, personality, freedom <1>p. 518</1> and self-determination with an intensity sufficient to justify reinforced legal containment <2>Laprano</2><3>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 152; p. 155)</3><4><5>520</5></4>. Along the same line, massive data exploitation, behavioral analysis and corporate surveillance show that these private powers operate today over central spheres of autonomy to a constitutionally relevant degree, requiring a more robust normative response <6>Mendes</6><7>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70; p. 72; p. 78)</7><8><9>521</9></8>. The <10>Lex Plataformae</10> does not govern only access and use; it may also govern the user's perception, predictability, exposure and margins of self-determination.

All this explains why the horizontal effect of fundamental rights, although indispensable, is still not enough on its own as an operational grammar of the problem. This constitutional containment must be brought back to a dogmatic language of control capable of touching, concretely, architecture, practices, information, sanction and evidentiary regimes. It is there that consumer law comes in, not as a sectoral appendix, but as a normative infrastructure for containing the asymmetries produced by the <1>Lex Plataformae</1>. The CDC starts precisely from the recognition that the supplier occupies a structurally preponderant position in defining the conditions of the bond, in organizing information, in modulating performance and in distributing risks, which is why vulnerability, good faith and balance operate as a <2>p. 519</2> concrete normative translation of the constitutional requirement to limit private power in the consumer relation <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 274; p. 324)</4><5><6>522</6></5>.

Under this key, the consumer contract ceases to be read as a neutral space of self-regulation and comes to be understood as a field for containing the supplier's dominant position. Objective good faith does not enter as decorative moralism, but as a technique for limiting the abusive exercise of private prerogatives, especially when projected onto a structurally vulnerable consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 111; p. 221)</2><3><4>523</4></3>. The platform may shape its service, but it may not convert this shaping into private sovereignty over the user's position. Likewise, the control of abusive clauses and practices in the CDC already offers sufficient language to bring the problem of platform governance down to the ground of positive law, typifying abuses, repressing exaggerated disadvantages and mitigating the fiction that everything accepted en masse has become legally legitimate <5>Miragem</5><6>(Miragem, 2020, p. 741; p. 370)</6><7><8>524</8></7>.

<1>p. 520</1> This consumer-law grammar appears clearly when one observes the normative doors opened by the legal provisions themselves. Strict liability for defects in the service and for insufficient or inadequate information<2><3>525</3></2>, the discipline of quality defects that make the service unfit or diminish its value<4><5>526</5></4> and the prohibition of abusive practices that take advantage of the consumer's weakness, impose excessive advantage or leave the performance of the obligation to the supplier's exclusive discretion<6><7>527</7></6> show that the problem of the <8>Lex Plataformae</8> need not be framed only as a lofty conflict between Constitution and market. It can already be grasped, operationally, as defect, inadequacy, abuse, exploitation of vulnerability and unilateral manipulation of the conditions of enjoyment. This shifts the focus from isolated clauses to structural patterns of governance, verifiability and reasoning.

The methodological consequence is decisive. The public relevance of the powers of the <1>Lex </1> <2>Plataformae</2> does not authorize confusing platform with State, but it prevents its governance from being read as an internal, legally neutral business detail. When a private supplier organizes, through <3>design</3> and <4>enforcement</4>, the conditions of access, permanence, equivalence, visibility, sanction and contestation of a continuous consumption experience, legal control cannot remain a prisoner of the contractual surface. It must reach the architecture of the relation and reintroduce, within it, criteria of controllability, reasoning and verifiability. Without this, opacity, unilateral mutation and systematic difficulties of contestation cease to appear as pathologies and come to be naturalized as the ordinary condition of digital consumption. It is precisely this naturalization that is refused here.

The incidence of fundamental rights in relations between private parties stems from the observation that socially relevant forms of oppression, inequality and subjection are not exhausted in State action, manifesting themselves also in private bonds organized by concentration of economic, technical, organizational and informational power <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 51)</2>. Fundamental legal protection cannot remain confined to the classic vertical scheme between State and individual, on pain of leaving legally uncovered precisely the contemporary forms of injury to freedom and to the sphere of the person that emerge in structurally asymmetric private relations. This reinforced incidence does not require falsifying the private relation as if it had been statized. The legally relevant point lies in recognizing that the Constitution is addressed to all and that fundamental rights shape the behavior of private parties when the exercise of private autonomy comes to relevantly affect another's legal sphere <3>Sarmento</3><4>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 258)</4>. In contexts of marked material inequality, the autonomy of the weaker subject tends to become fictitious, which is why the expansion of the protection of fundamental rights in the private sphere functions as a response to the real asymmetry of power between the parties <5>Sarmento</5><6>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 285)</6>. The platform need not be treated as the State for its powers to be legally shapeable. It is enough to recognize that, in structurally asymmetric and socially relevant private relations, private autonomy no longer operates as an absolute shield against the incidence of fundamental rights. <7>↩</7>

The application of fundamental rights to private relations does not presuppose the artificial transformation of the private party into a State entity, but stems from the need to protect the person against the power concretely exercised by another private party. What justifies the binding effect is not the formal nature of the agent, but the impossibility of treating private law as a space set apart from the Constitution, immune to the normative force of fundamental rights <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 528-529)</2>. Private autonomy does not function as automatic shielding whenever the contractual or organizational relation is structured on materially asymmetric bases. In this sense, at least some effect of fundamental rights on the private sphere must be recognized precisely to prevent private norms, clauses, powers or practices from contradicting the fundamental-rights content constitutionally ensured to the person <3>Sarlet</3><4>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 528; p. 530)</4>. The point is strong because it dismantles the old fiction according to which it would be enough to call the relation “private” to remove it from the field of constitutional shaping. The platform remains a private party, the relation remains private and private law continues to exist; what disappears is the claim to immunity founded only on this formal qualification. Thus, the legal containment of the powers of the Lex Plataformae stems from protecting the person against the private power exercised over them, and not from the need to pretend that this power has become State power. <5>↩</5>

The legal containment of private powers with public relevance does not depend on an artificial equation between private party and State, but on the perception that the simple privatization of the activity or of the infrastructure of power cannot reduce the scope of incidence of fundamental rights <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 61)</2>. The private nature of the agent has no magic force to expel the Constitution from the relation, above all when the power exercised by this agent reaches an intensity sufficient to condition choices, restrict freedoms and structurally affect the practical position of the individuals submitted to its architecture of governance. At the same time, this containment does not require dissolving the private nature of the relation nor transplanting the State's legal regime entirely onto the private party. The question lies in recognizing that the private party is also a holder of fundamental rights and of autonomy, but that this autonomy ceases to be absolute when the exercise of its power relevantly affects the fundamental rights of third parties <3>Sarmento</3><4>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 209)</4>. Even outside the strict cases of exercise of a public function, the concrete public relevance of the power exercised matters legally, because the material impact of this power on another's sphere justifies reinforced constitutional containment <5>Sarmento</5><6>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 298)</6>. The <7>Lex </7> <8>Plataformae</8> need not be treated as an arm of the State for its powers to be limited. It is enough to recognize that, when a private agent concentrates economic, technical, informational and organizational power sufficient to structurally affect the user's freedom and material equality, private autonomy can no longer function as an absolute safe-conduct. <9>↩</9>

The incidence of fundamental rights in relations between private parties becomes especially clear when private autonomy ceases to operate in a scenario of minimally real parity and comes to cover materially asymmetric bonds. In consumer relations, the structural inequality between the parties prevents contractual freedom from being treated as a self-sufficient criterion for legitimizing the bond, requiring reinforced legal containment in favor of the vulnerable party <1>Santos</1><2>(Santos, 2019, p. 15)</2>. The platform need not be equated with the State for its action to cease being read as a sovereign sphere immune to legal control. It is enough that the relation it structures concentrates relevant power on one side and vulnerability on the other. This key is reinforced when the asymmetry between the subjects of the relation is taken as a parameter for intensifying the protective incidence of fundamental rights. The more unequal the private relation, the smaller the legitimate space for an absolutized reading of negotiating autonomy and the greater the need to protect the fundamental right affected <3>Santos</3><4>(Santos, 2019, p. 112; p. 132)</4>. Therefore, the public relevance of the powers of the <5>Lex Plataformae </5>does not derive from a fiction that transforms the platform into a State entity, but from the observation that, in structurally asymmetric private relations, private autonomy can no longer function as a screen to shield the exercise of economic, technical and informational power over the user. <6>↩</6>

The legal containment of private powers exercised in a platform environment finds, in the consumer-law microsystem, a concrete form of normative translation of the requirement of material balance in relations between private parties. Instead of treating the contract as a neutral space of self-regulation between formally equivalent wills, consumer law starts from the recognition that the supplier occupies a structurally preponderant position in defining the conditions of the bond, in organizing information, in modulating performance and in distributing risks. Marques formulates this shift by stating that, in consumer societies, "it is no longer believed that by ensuring the autonomy of the will and contractual freedom the necessary harmony and equity in contractual relations will automatically be achieved", highlighting that standardized methods of contracting make "clear the imbalance between the contracting parties", which is why it fell to the State to intervene to restore balance and equality of forces <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 42)</2>. This logic is especially useful for reading the Lex Plataformae, because it shows that the platform's private governance is not exhausted in internally legitimate business choices, but produces concrete effects on the consumer's enjoyment, permanence and self-determination. In a convergent sense, Marques defines abusiveness as "imbalance or mismatch of rights and obligations between the parties", associated with the authorization of action contrary to good faith and with the abuse of the preponderant contractual position <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 162)</4>. In this key, the horizontal effect of fundamental rights is brought back, on the consumer-law plane, to the containment of the supplier's dominant position. <5>↩</5>

Private autonomy cannot be understood, in a constitutional key, as an abstract safe-conduct for the exercise of private power in contexts of material inequality. When the relation between private parties is organized on non-paritarian terms, the purely formal invocation of contractual freedom is no longer enough to legitimize the bond, because the absence of ostensive coercion does not equate, by itself, to the existence of real freedom to decide, resist or negotiate under minimally equivalent conditions <1>Sarmento</1><2>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 183)</2>. Private autonomy is relativized not out of hostility to the market or to the contract, but because its legitimacy depends on material conditions that allow its effective exercise. This relativization acquires even greater density when one recognizes that material equality, inferred from the Constitution, imposes protection of the weaker parties in private relations, which necessarily compresses the space of a private autonomy read in absolute terms <3>Sarmento</3><4>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 286)</4>. In a scenario of acute social inequality, the fiction of legal equality between individuals cannot serve to shield more powerful private parties against the incidence of fundamental rights, above all when the invocation of private autonomy comes to mask relations of material subordination <5>Sarmento</5><6>(Sarmento, 2010, p. 51)</6>. The legal containment of the private powers of platforms does not violate private autonomy. On the contrary, it prevents it from being mobilized as an elegant formula to legitimize the material subjection of the vulnerable user before private structures of concentrated power. <7>↩</7>

The incidence of fundamental rights in relations between private parties is justified when the threat to freedom, to material equality and to the sphere of the person ceases to come only from the State and comes to emerge also from private centers of social and economic power intense enough to produce relevant subjection <1>Sarlet</1><2>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 527)</2>. The private relation does not become constitutionally immune merely because it does not involve direct State action, above all when the concrete structure of the bond reveals a concentration of power apt to pressure, condition or restrict the practical freedom of the weaker subject. This reinforced incidence does not require confusing company with State. What is legally relevant is to recognize that, in the private sphere too, situations of inequality occur that are produced by the asymmetric exercise of social power, which is why aggressions against individual freedom and against the human-dignity content of fundamental rights cannot be tolerated merely because they are practiced by private parties <3>Sarlet</3><4>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 529)</4>. In manifestly unequal relations, doctrine itself admits the transposition to the private sphere of principles linked to the binding effect of fundamental rights, precisely because one is facing structures of power functionally comparable, in their asymmetry, to the relations between individual and public power <5>Sarlet</5><6>(Sarlet, 2018, p. 530)</6>. The public relevance of the powers of the <7>Lex Plataformae</7> does not depend on “statizing” the platform, but on recognizing that its concentration of technical, economic, informational and organizational power may reach the user's sphere with constitutionally relevant intensity. <8>↩</8>

The exploitation of personal data by private digital agents cannot be treated as an entirely self-referential sphere, because data constitute legally relevant projections of personality and their protection is linked, ultimately, to the protection of human dignity and informational self-determination. Along this line, data protection imposes a genuine obligation on the processing agent to respect the data subject's informational self-determination, precisely because personal data constitute an extension of their personality, protected by the constitutional centrality of human dignity <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155)</2>. The same key appears when it is stated that the guarantee of protection of personal data, whether through the discipline of the LGPD or through the incidence of the horizontal effect of fundamental rights in the concrete case, especially those linked to privacy and personality, aims, ultimately, at protecting the fundamental rights of the data subject <3>Laprano</3><4>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 156)</4>. For this reason, the infraconstitutional protection of personal data can be understood as an expression of the mediate horizontal effect of the fundamental rights of freedom, privacy and free development of the natural person, opening space for a more direct incidence of these principles in private relations <5>Laprano</5><6>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 156)</6>. The public relevance of the powers of the Lex Plataformae, thus, already finds support in the articulation between personal data, personality and the horizontal effect of fundamental rights. <7>↩</7>

The reinforced legal containment of digitally mediated private powers does not stem from theoretical voluntarism, but from the observation that the information society and private structures of surveillance have imposed the recognition and explicit statement of new fundamental rights, especially the protection of personal data and informational self-determination. Along this line, the development of information and communication technologies, in a surveillance society marked by the mitigation of privacy, imposed the need to reflect on new fundamental rights <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 69-70)</2>. The same key is reinforced when one recognizes that the economic exploitation of personal data without sufficient consent did not remain only on the infraconstitutional plane, the case law of the STF having confirmed the existence of autonomous fundamental rights to the protection of personal data and to informational self-determination <3>Mendes</3><4>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 82-83)</4>. In addition, these rights are understood as the result of an evolutive interpretation of privacy, whose protection had to be reconfigured to maintain effectiveness in the surveillance society <5>Mendes</5><6>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 78-79)</6>. The public relevance of the powers of the <7>Lex Plataformae</7>, thus, also becomes evident because private surveillance and massive data processing already operate, in the contemporary informational environment, as phenomena apt to justify reinforced constitutional containment. <8>↩</8>

Private powers exercised in digital environments bear on legally protected projections of personality and, for that reason, cannot be read as spheres immune to constitutional control. Data protection, in this key, ceases to be a purely market question and comes to operate as a form of defense of the person against private forms of interference in their informational and decision-making life. In this direction, the protection of personality rights is not exhausted in their enactment in the Civil Code, also having the stature of fundamental rights, which allows data protection itself to be understood as a form of defense of these rights <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 152)</2>. The same reasoning is reinforced when the problem is situated in the tension between an impersonal market and the protection of the fundamental rights of the natural person submitted to such influences, in a perspective of repersonalization of private law <3>Laprano</3><4>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141)</4>. In cases of justifiable vulnerability, even the immediate use of the fundamental norm, in its pure form, is admitted to make possible the effective rebalancing between the parties <5>Laprano</5><6>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 155)</6>. The limitation of digitally mediated private powers can be built through the articulation of personality rights, data protection, vulnerability and horizontal effect. <7>↩</7>

Digitally mediated private powers produce sufficient impact on privacy, behavior, personality and autonomy to justify reinforced legal containment in light of fundamental rights. In a surveillance society, the enormous quantity of personal data converted into information about personality and intimacy, and used by companies for behavioral analysis, calls into question the very possibility of preserving privacy <1>Mendes</1><2>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 70)</2>. When private structures accumulate the capacity to infer, monitor and exploit such deep dimensions of individuals' lives, one is no longer facing mere neutral business freedom and moves onto the terrain of the exercise of socially relevant power over fundamental goods. This reading deepens when one recognizes, in dialogue with Shoshana Zuboff, that the power derived from the extraction and analysis of personal data reaches the capacity to shape human behavior, requiring responses of containment and regulation of surveillance capitalism <3>Mendes</3><4>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 72)</4>. In addition, the existence of abuses committed by technology companies reinforces the need for more robust protection of data processing relations, including in digital media <5>Mendes</5><6>(Canavez; Santos; Mendes, 2022, p. 78)</6>. The reinforced incidence of fundamental rights, therefore, is justified because these private powers already operate over central spheres of autonomy with legally relevant intensity. <7>↩</7>

The containment of private powers in the consumer environment does not depend only on abstract constitutional theory, because it already finds operable language within the CDC itself. The consumer's subjective right to contractual balance stems directly from consumer-law principles, in particular good faith, vulnerability and balance itself. Because of the consumer's vulnerability before the supplier, who holds a dominant position in the contract, the CDC establishes a series of norms limiting the supplier's private power, through clear State legislative intervention in contractual autonomy, aimed at protecting the interests of the vulnerable party <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 274)</2>. This reading gains density when one recognizes that, in contemporary society, the consumer relation presents itself less as an expression of contractual freedom and more as the fulfillment of a need to consume. In this context, the notion of abuse translates the prevalence of the supplier's dominant position over the consumer's vulnerability, good faith being the central legal brake on the exercise of this negotiating superiority <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 324)</4>. The public relevance of the powers of the Lex Plataformae, therefore, need not remain suspended in a theoretical cloud: it can already be grasped in a key of structural vulnerability, good faith, balance and limitation of abuse within the real CDC. <5>↩</5>

Objective good faith, in the consumer contract, does not act as a moral ornament, but as a concrete technique for containing the abusive exercise of private prerogatives, especially when these are projected onto a structurally vulnerable party. In contexts of informational asymmetry, practical dependence and unilateral predisposition of the rules of the bond, consumer protection requires that the exercise of contractual powers be submitted to parameters of loyalty, reasonableness, economic and social purpose and respect for the trust legitimately placed in the relation. This is exactly the point developed by Marques when stating that "the notion of objective good faith, as a new principle guiding the conduct of the contracting parties in captive contracts, means a new and important limitation on the exercise of subjective rights", so that the exercise of the right will be abusive when diverted from its economic and social function or exercised in disloyal circumstances <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 111)</2>. The author adds that good faith has a limiting function, "reducing the freedom of action of the contractual partners" and controlling abusive conduct and clauses <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 221)</4>. In a platform environment, this prevents the freedom to shape the bond from being converted into private sovereignty over the consumer's position. <5>↩</5>

The control of abusive clauses and practices functions, in the CDC, as a direct technique for containing structural asymmetries between consumer and supplier. Arts. 39 and 51 make up protective mechanisms designed precisely to equalize a factually unequal relation, typifying abusive practices and sanctioning abusive clauses with nullity by operation of law, in a clear mitigation of pacta sunt servanda <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 741)</2>. Abusiveness, in this key, does not appear as a peripheral deviation or a moral correction of occasional excesses, but as a legislative instrument for repressing the disloyal exercise of dominant private positions. This control thickens when one perceives that abuse of right, in consumer law, corresponds above all to the abuse of a dominant legal position of the supplier in the consumer market. It is the exploitation of this superior position over the consumer's vulnerability that qualifies certain practices and stipulations as abusive, whether on the plane of conduct or on the plane of contractual content that imposes exaggerated disadvantage on the adhering party <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 370)</4>. In practical terms, the containment of the platform need not be built only through lofty constitutional mediation: good faith, abuse of dominant position, exaggerated disadvantage and the nullity of abusive clauses already offer sufficient grammar to bring it down to the ground of the CDC. <5>↩</5>

<1>6.1.3 </1>On personal integrity, symbolic identity and biographical continuity as reference legal interests

The continued enjoyment of the Immaterial Object of Consumption cannot be adequately grasped when reduced to the language of immediate utility or of the price paid. In platform-governed ecosystems, what the consumer maintains over time is not only functional access to a digital performance, but a position of enjoyment that incorporates history, memory, recognition, identity projection and practical continuity of presence in the environment. The corresponding legal protection, therefore, cannot be blind to the circumstance that certain losses, erasures, sanctions and unilateral reconfigurations reach not only the economic value of the acquisition, but also dimensions of personal integrity and symbolic identity that become objectified in the very course of the digital experience. The rereading of private law in light of human dignity long ago broke with the narrow view that confined the legal problem to the patrimonial value of the good affected, requiring attention to the existential projections of the person in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 10; p. 17)</2><3><4>561</4></3>.

<1>p. 535</1> This does not mean dissolving the analysis into academic sentimentalism, an elegant shortcut for thinking ill of the one whose conduct is now being questioned. The question at hand is more sober. In platform environments, the consumer's personality is cut up into data, profiles, histories, metrics, reputations and trails of participation that condition concrete possibilities of permanence, recognition and self-determination. The digital experience may reach legally relevant dimensions of personal integrity precisely because data protection, informational self-determination and the free development of personality form part of the existential core of the person in an informational environment <2>Laprano</2><3>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 139; p. 148; p. 155-156)</3><4><5>562</5></4>. That is why the administration of these elements cannot be treated as a simple “data issue” set apart from the consumer relation. It forms part of the very regime of enjoyment and interferes directly with the consumer's informational and biographical integrity.
